section.title: God's Love for Israel
section.sectionRationale: After chapters of accumulating judgment, the tone breaks open into the tenderest revelation of God's heart in the book. God remembers Israel as a beloved child He taught to walk, and though justice demands ruin, His compassion recoils within Him. Here is the wounded, pursuing love of God, and the words Matthew will apply to Christ.
section.thesis: Though Israel spurned the Father who called His son out of Egypt and taught him to walk, God's compassion overrides His wrath, for He is God and not man, the Holy One who will not give His people up.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Father's remembered love for His child; the child's stubborn turning away; and the divine heart that recoils, refusing to give Ephraim up.

units.label: Out of Egypt I called My son
units.note: the Father who taught him to walk

verses.text: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My {{ben|son}}.
But the more I called Israel, the farther they departed from Me. They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images.
It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by the arms, but they never realized that it was I who healed them.
I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of {{ahavah|love}}; I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them.

units.label: The child who would not return

verses.text: Will they not return to the land of Egypt and be ruled by Assyria because they refused to repent?
A sword will flash through their cities; it will destroy the bars of their gates and consume them in their own plans.
My people are bent on turning from Me. Though they call to the Most High, He will by no means exalt them.

units.label: How can I give you up?

verses.text: How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel? How could I make you like Admah? How could I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart is turned within Me; My {{nicham|compassion}} is stirred!
I will not execute the full fury of My anger; I will not destroy Ephraim again. For I am God and not man, the Holy One among you, and I will not come in wrath.
They will walk after the LORD; He will roar like a lion. When He roars, His children will come trembling from the west.
They will come trembling like birds from Egypt and like doves from the land of Assyria. Then I will settle them in their homes, declares the LORD.
Ephraim surrounds Me with lies, the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One.

ben.gloss: A son, a child. God calls Israel His son whom He called out of Egypt, framing the exodus as the rescue of a beloved child. Matthew 2:15 applies this very phrase to Jesus, the true and faithful Son, showing that Israel's story is taken up and fulfilled in Christ.

ahavah.gloss: Love, affection. Here it is the fatherly, tender love with which God led Israel, with cords of kindness and ropes of love, lifting the yoke and stooping to feed His child. It reveals that God's dealings with His people flow from deep affection, not cold obligation.

nicham.gloss: To be moved to compassion, to relent, to have one's heart change toward mercy. In verse 8 God's compassion is stirred, His heart recoils within Him, and He turns from executing the full fury of His wrath. It expresses the astonishing depth of divine mercy that overrides deserved judgment.

basic.context: The thunder of judgment gives way to the tenderest words in Hosea. God remembers Israel as a little child He loved and called out of Egypt, whom He taught to walk, holding him by the arms and bending down to feed him. But the child kept running away to idols. Justice would rightly destroy them as it destroyed Admah and Zeboiim near Sodom. Yet God cries out, How can I give you up? His heart recoils within Him, His compassion is stirred, and He declares He will not carry out the full fury of His anger, for He is God and not man.
basic.hermeneutics: This is deeply anthropomorphic poetry, portraying God's inner life in human terms so we can grasp the reality of His love and mercy. Verse 9, I am God and not man, guards against misreading: God's mercy is not fickle human sentiment but the steadfast, holy love of God Himself. Matthew 2:15 reads verse 1 as fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel and Son.
basic.originalLanguages: God calls Israel His ben, His son, called out of Egypt, a phrase Matthew applies to Jesus. He led them with ahavah, tender love, cords of kindness. And at the climax His nicham, compassion, is stirred so that His heart recoils from wrath. Son, love, and relenting compassion together open the very heart of God.
basic.typology: Out of Egypt I called My son is directly fulfilled in Christ, whom Matthew shows recapitulating and redeeming Israel's story. Where the son Israel was faithless, Jesus the true Son is faithful. God's refusal to give His people up, absorbing rather than executing the full fury of wrath, foreshadows the cross, where wrath and mercy meet and God saves His people at cost to Himself.
basic.christ: Matthew takes the words out of Egypt I called My son and applies them to Jesus, the true Son who succeeds where Israel failed and so redeems His people. The mystery of verse 8, God's compassion overriding His wrath, is not sentimentality; it finds its resolution at the cross. There God does not simply set His justice aside; He satisfies it in His Son, so that He can righteously refuse to give His people up. The Holy One among you who will not come in wrath is the God who comes in Christ to bear the wrath Himself.
basic.god: This chapter reveals the heart of God more nakedly than almost any other. He is a Father whose love goes back to His people's infancy, who is genuinely grieved by their rebellion, and whose compassion recoils at the thought of their ruin. He is holy, and precisely because He is God and not man His mercy is deeper and more constant than any human love. His love does not ignore sin, but it will not let His people go.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 2:15 applies out of Egypt I called My son to Christ. Romans 5 shows God demonstrating His love in Christ's death for sinners. Lamentations 3 and Deuteronomy 29:23 illuminate God's compassions and the fate of Admah and Zeboiim.
basic.oneStory: Chapter 11 unveils the Father heart of God, who called His son out of Egypt and cannot bear to give His people up. The whole Bible answers this in Christ, the true Son called out of Egypt, in whom God's wrath is borne and His compassion triumphs, so that His people are settled home forever.

context.literary:
Chapter 11 is a single poem with a rise, a break and a recovery. Verses 1 to 4 are a memory told in the past tense, a father's recollection of a child's early years. Verses 5 to 7 move to the future with a sentence of exile and the sword. Then verses 8 and 9 break the pattern. The questions of verse 8, four of them in a row, are the clearest place in the book where God deliberates aloud, and the answers of verse 9 are a string of negatives: I will not execute, I will not destroy, I will not come in wrath. Verses 10 and 11 then close in the future tense with a restoration, and the last verse, verse 12, returns to the present with a short line of charge and a surprising note about Judah.

The central device is the contrast between what God did and what Israel did. The first four verses repeat a simple pattern: I loved, I called, I taught, I led, I lifted, I fed. The verbs of the people are few and bleak, they sacrificed, they burned incense, they did not realize. A reader can feel the imbalance, a long catalogue of care set against a handful of refusals, and the effect is to make the rebellion look not only wrong but ungrateful.

The poem also plays with the image of the father. It begins in infancy, moves through teaching a child to walk and feeding him, and shifts to a farm animal whose yoke is eased. By verse 8 the father is wrestling with the law's demand, because Deuteronomy 21:18 to 21 describes how a rebellious son might be dealt with. The questions of verse 8 are the father's refusal to carry out that sentence.

The chapter forms a pair with the lawsuit speeches around it. Chapters 9 and 10 end in destruction and chapter 12 returns to accusation. Chapter 11 is a pocket of tenderness set in the middle of the book's most severe stretch, and the placement is deliberate.
context.historical:
Hosea writes with the exodus as the great founding memory. The call out of Egypt was the event by which Israel became a nation, and Exodus 4:22 had already named Israel the LORD's firstborn son. Hosea reaches back to that moment and treats it as the start of a relationship, not just a rescue. The Baals of verse 2 are the local fertility gods that dominated Canaanite agricultural religion, and the incense and carved images belong to the worship at the northern shrines that Hosea attacks throughout.

The threat of verse 5 reflects the political reality of the 730s and 720s BC. Assyria was the dominant power, and Israel had been alternating between paying tribute to it and seeking help from Egypt, Hosea 7:11. The prophet foresees that the nation which turned to both will be ruled by the one, and the sword of verse 6 refers to the invasions that destroyed city after city. The gate bars were what a city relied on for defence, and their breaking implies that no walls will hold.

The cities of verse 8, Admah and Zeboiim, are not often mentioned. They belonged to the cities of the plain, were allied with Sodom and Gomorrah, Genesis 14:2, and are named in Deuteronomy 29:23 as examples of total overthrow, a burning waste of sulfur and salt. By choosing them rather than Sodom, Hosea invokes a memory that every Israelite knew from the law, and he asks whether Israel should suffer the fate that the law threatened.

The return in verses 10 and 11 draws on the image of Israelites coming back from the nations. Egypt and Assyria were the two places where Israelites had been or would be held, and the scattered people coming home like birds describes the full gathering. The lion that roars is the picture the prophets use for the LORD in judgment, and here it is turned into a summons. The hearers who first heard this were living in a land under threat, and verse 11 gave them a promise of homes.
context.canonical:
Hosea 11:1 is quoted once in the New Testament, at Matthew 2:15, where Joseph brings the child Jesus out of Egypt after Herod's death. The wider setting of the passage is picked up again and again in the Old Testament. Exodus 4:22 calls Israel the LORD's firstborn son, Deuteronomy 32:10 to 12 describes the LORD as an eagle that stirs the nest and carries its young, and Isaiah 46:3 and 4 speaks of a people carried from birth who will be carried to old age. Isaiah 63:9 says of the exodus that in His love and compassion He redeemed them, He lifted them up and carried them. Hosea 11 is a sibling of these passages and the most intimate of them.

The thought of God's heart being turned within Him has close parallels. Jeremiah 31:20 uses nearly the same terms: Is not Ephraim a precious son to Me, a delightful child? Though I often speak against him, I still remember him. Therefore My heart yearns for him. Isaiah 49:15 asks whether a woman can forget her nursing child, and answers that God will not forget. Lamentations 3:31 to 33 says the Lord will not cast off forever and does not willingly afflict. These passages show that Hosea is stating something central to the prophetic understanding of God, not an isolated mood.

The answer to how God can refuse to give His people up while remaining just is worked out in the New Testament. Romans 3:25 and 26 shows God demonstrating His righteousness in the atoning sacrifice, so that He is both just and the one who justifies. Romans 8:32 says He did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. The question of verse 8, how can I give you up, is answered by the gift of the Son in their place. Galatians 4:4 to 7 and Romans 8:14 and 15 take the language of sonship and apply it to believers, who are adopted as sons and cry Abba Father.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hosea intended this poem as the heart of his message, the place where the covenant lawsuit shows what lies behind it. His hearers had been told in chapters 4 to 10 what they had done and what would follow. Here they are told how God feels about it, and the purpose is to break the idea that He is a distant judge who wants only to punish. The intent is to make them hear the voice of a parent who has been wounded.

The prophet also wanted to explain why there is any future at all. Judgment has already been announced, and a reader might have supposed that nothing remained. Verse 9 gives the reason in the nature of God Himself: He is God and not man, the Holy One in their midst. The hope does not rest on Israel's improvement. It rests on who God is, and the first hearers were meant to find in that fact a ground for hope that no failure of their own could remove.

And he meant his hearers to be moved to return. The tender memory is not offered as an excuse for continued rebellion but as a reason to stop. The one who taught Ephraim to walk is the one to whom Ephraim must now walk back, and the closing picture of trembling birds coming home is an invitation as well as a promise.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter describes the inner life of God in the language of a parent, and it describes a historical judgment, the exile, and a future restoration. It does not prescribe a method for raising children, though many parents have found it wise, and it does not tell the reader that God will never discipline. Verses 5 to 7 are just as much a part of the poem as verses 8 and 9, and a reading that keeps the mercy while dropping the sword has stopped listening.\n\nThe application belongs where the passage itself puts it, in how God's people think of Him. We are meant to believe that He is not a reluctant giver of mercy but a Father whose heart is moved. We are also meant to read the language about God's heart as accommodated, as 'I am God and not man' in verse 9 demands, so that we do not suppose He is torn like a human parent who does not know what to do. The poem teaches that God's love is real and costly, while the rest of Scripture shows how the cost is met.

debates.question: How does Matthew use Hosea 11:1 when he applies it to Jesus?

views.label: Typological fulfilment: Jesus as the true Israel
views.case: Hosea is plainly looking back at the exodus, so Matthew is reading the verse by pattern. Israel was God's son called out of Egypt, and Jesus, who is the Son, retraces Israel's path and succeeds where Israel failed. Matthew often builds his Gospel on such correspondences, and this one is signalled by the movement into Egypt and out again.

views.label: A prophecy hidden in a historical statement
views.case: Some older interpreters treated the verse as a direct prediction of the Messiah's journey. The difficulty is that Hosea speaks in the past tense of Israel's history and goes on in verse 2 to describe Israel's sin, which cannot be said of Jesus.

views.label: A loose verbal accommodation
views.case: Others hold that Matthew only borrows the words because they fit, without seeing any real connection. This struggles with the fact that Matthew's opening chapters repeatedly present Jesus as one who sums up Israel's story, and with the way the New Testament reads the Old as promise.

debates.bearing: The first view best fits both Hosea and Matthew. The verse is about Israel, and Jesus is Israel's representative, so that what is said of the people is true in fullness of the One who stands for them.

debates.question: If God is not a man that He should change His mind, how can verse 8 say that His heart is turned within Him?

views.label: Real emotion, unchanging purpose
views.case: Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say God is not a man that He should change His mind, yet Scripture often says He relents, as in Exodus 32:14. On this view God's character and covenant purposes are fixed, while the way He relates to His people responds to their repentance and need, and the language of heart and compassion is a true if accommodated expression of that.

views.label: Anthropomorphic figure only
views.case: Others emphasise that language of heart turning and compassion stirring is a figure of speech, an accommodation to human understanding, and that the passage is really about God's settled disposition of mercy. Verse 9, I am God and not man, is the key that tells us to read verse 8 this way.

debates.bearing: Both views guard what the passage guards, that God's mercy does not come from a change in His nature. The poem lets us hear the real love of a Father without suggesting that He is fickle, and the closing lines of verse 9 tell us the reason is who He is.

debates.question: What is the meaning of verse 12 about Judah?

views.label: Judah is still faithful
views.case: The BSB reads that Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One, setting the south against the deceit of the north. Judah did at times have faithful kings, as in the reforms of Hezekiah.

views.label: Judah is also unruly
views.case: The BSB footnote offers another reading, that Judah is unruly against God, the faithful Holy One. On this reading the verse widens the charge, and 12:2 does turn to a charge against Judah.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew is hard, and honest translators divide. Either way, the verse reminds the reader that the LORD's mercy for the north does not erase the claim He has on the south.

study.originalLanguages:
The tender verb of verse 3 is built on the Hebrew word for foot, regel, and conveys the picture of a father making a toddler walk, steadying the child step by step. The exodus and wilderness story is told here as the childhood of a nation, and the care is detailed, close and physical. In the same verse the LORD says that He healed them, using the verb rapha, which Hosea uses again at 6:1 and 14:4, so that the memory of healing is bracketed by the promise of healing to come.

The striking verb of verse 8 is the one in the clause "My heart is turned within Me." It is the same root that Deuteronomy 29:23 uses for the overthrow of Admah and Zeboiim, and that Genesis 19:25 uses for the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah. The word for overturn is turned inward: the destruction that God might have rained on the people is felt as an upheaval in His own heart. It is one of the most daring plays on a word in the prophets, and it makes the point that the wrath is absorbed internally before it is meted out.

Verse 9 turns on the contrast between "God" and "man." The Hebrew sets el, God, against ish, a man, and the contrast is that of Numbers 23:19. The Holy One is described as "among you," in your midst, which links the word of mercy to the presence of God in the camp. His holiness is the ground of the mercy, not its limit. A human being would act out of anger and be done. The Holy One remains, and remaining is what makes mercy possible.

The verb in "I will not destroy Ephraim again" is shuv, the word for turn or return, which is the same verb the prophets use for Israel's repentance. Here God's own turning is the subject, and the verb that Israel has refused is applied to God, who will not turn to destroy. The roar of verse 10 uses the verb of the lion, which in Hosea 5:14 and 13:7 was a figure of attack. Now the lion roars to call the children home, and they come trembling, a word for a quaking that is part fear and part awe.

Finally, verse 11 says "I will settle them" using the verb yashav, to cause to dwell. The refugees who fly like birds do not merely arrive; they are given homes. The language moves from exile to residence, and it is the opposite of the wandering of chapter 9.

typology.type: Israel the son called out of Egypt
typology.fulfillment: The exodus made Israel the LORD's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22. Matthew shows Jesus passing through Egypt and out again, 2:15, so that the pattern of Israel's origin is lived again by the true Son. The correspondence deepens in the wilderness, where He is tested for forty days and answers from the same book that Israel had failed, Matthew 4:1 to 4. The escalation is that Israel was a son by adoption and grace, but Jesus is the Son by nature, Luke 3:22. The type falls short because Israel's sonship could not by itself bring the nations in, while Christ's does, Galatians 4:4 to 5.

typology.type: The father who taught a child to walk and bent down to feed him
typology.fulfillment: The care of verses 3 and 4 is a type of the Father's care for His people, finally revealed in the Son. Jesus shows the Father in His own acts, feeding the multitudes, and in the parable of the loving father who runs to meet a returning son, Luke 15:20. The Father's compassion in the parable is the narrative form of Hosea 11:8. It falls short in that the care in the poem could not make the people respond, whereas in Christ the Spirit of sonship is given so that believers cry out, Abba, Father, Romans 8:15.

typology.type: The overturned heart and the cities of the plain
typology.fulfillment: Admah and Zeboiim stand for the full outpouring of wrath, and God's heart is turned within Him instead of the cities being turned over. The pattern of the wrath being absorbed is completed at the cross, where the Son is given up so that His people are not, Romans 8:32. The Father who said how can I give you up gave up His own Son, and in that giving He remained just, Romans 3:26. The type is only partial because Hosea does not say how the wrath is carried, and only the cross makes that plain.

typology.type: The lion who roars and the children who come home
typology.fulfillment: The roar that once announced judgment becomes a summons, and the exiles come trembling like doves from the nations. Christ is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Revelation 5:5, who triumphs by being the slain Lamb, and He gathers the scattered children of God into one, John 11:52. The correspondence reaches its height in the gathering of people from every nation, tribe and tongue, Revelation 7:9. The type is incomplete because Hosea speaks of the return of the exiles from Egypt and Assyria, while the full ingathering is wider and still unfolding.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the quoted verse. When Matthew says that the flight to Egypt fulfilled "Out of Egypt I called My Son," he is claiming that the story of Israel finds its meaning in Jesus. Israel was a child loved and called, and she ran after the Baals. Jesus is the Son who passes through the same places and does not run. He is baptized and heard by the Father as the beloved Son, Luke 3:22, is led into the wilderness where Israel had failed, and answers every test from the Scriptures that Israel had ignored, Matthew 4:1 to 4. The pattern Hosea lamented is reversed in Him.

It leads to Christ by the question of verse 8. How can God give up Ephraim, and how can He not? If He executes the full fury of His anger, the people are consumed. If He simply relents, His justice looks hollow. The New Testament resolves the tension at the cross. God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, Romans 8:32, and He presented Him as the atoning sacrifice, to demonstrate His righteousness and so be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:25 and 26. The Father refused to give up Ephraim by giving up the Son. The heart that was turned within Him was turned toward the cross.

It leads to Christ by the wrath that is not executed. Verse 9 says, "I will not come in wrath." In Christ this becomes concrete. The wrath that was due falls on Him, Isaiah 53:5, and those who are in Him are told that there is now no condemnation, Romans 8:1. Paul says that God proves His love in this, that while we were still sinners Christ died for us, Romans 5:8. Hosea shows the love of God in poetry, and the cross shows it in blood.

It leads to Christ by the gathering. The roaring of the LORD and the children coming trembling from the west are fulfilled when the Lion of Judah calls His sheep, and they hear His voice, John 10:16. The one who gathers is the one who was born in Bethlehem and carried to Egypt and called out of it. His name, Jesus, means the LORD saves, and the same Matthew who quotes Hosea 11:1 records the name given to Joseph, Matthew 1:21.

The care needed here is plain. Hosea did not write a prophecy that mentioned Bethlehem or Herod, and Matthew does not claim that he did. The connection is by Israel's representative: what is said of the nation is true of the One who stands for the nation. And the poem's heart, the Father who will not give up His child, is not a reading imposed on the text, but the very thing the New Testament says was proved at the cross.
study.god:
The poem is one of the great windows into the character of God. It opens by showing that He initiates. Israel did not seek Him; He loved the child and called him out. Deuteronomy 7:7 and 8 says the LORD did not set His affection on Israel because they were large or deserving, but because He loved them, and Hosea 11:1 is the same truth in the form of a family story. The origin of the relationship is entirely in God, and that is the foundation of everything that follows.

The chapter shows a God who is personal and affected. His heart is turned, His compassion is stirred, and He asks questions as a father does when he cannot bring himself to do what is just by itself. This is the language of involvement, and it rules out any picture of a God who is indifferent or machine-like. Yet it is held together with the sharp contrast of verse 9: He is God and not man. The same Lord whose heart turns also does not change in who He is. His mercy is not mood but nature, and that is why it can be trusted.

The chapter also shows that God's holiness and His mercy are not opposed. Many people suppose that a holy God must be a God of anger and that mercy needs a softening of holiness. Hosea says the opposite: because He is the Holy One in their midst, He will not come in wrath. His holiness is the otherness that rises above human vindictiveness. A mere man in the same situation would give way to anger and destroy, but the Holy One is able to keep His purposes and spare.

The poem allows a real severity to remain. The sword will flash and exile will come. God does not deny the sin or cancel the consequences, and verses 5 to 7 stand in the text. What He refuses is the total end. The refusal means that His discipline is never the last word, and that a remnant, a return and a home are held in reserve. This agrees with what He says of Himself in Exodus 34:6 and 7, compassionate and gracious, and yet not leaving the guilty unpunished.

The worship that follows is trust. A God like this is not to be approached with the cringing of those who fear a tyrant, nor with the casualness of those who think He cannot be offended. He is to be approached with the trembling confidence of children who know they have wronged a father who has not stopped loving them. The picture of the birds coming home trembling holds both the fear and the joy.

crossReferences.note: Joseph takes the child Jesus to Egypt and brings Him back, and Matthew says this fulfilled Out of Egypt I called My Son. Hosea's verse is about the exodus, and Matthew shows Jesus living Israel's story from its beginning, the true Son who comes through Egypt and does not rebel.

The LORD tells Moses to say to Pharaoh that Israel is My firstborn son and that he must let My son go. This is the root of Hosea 11:1. The call out of Egypt was a rescue of a son, and Pharaoh's refusal was a refusal to release the Father's child.

The LORD found Israel in a desert land and cared for him like an eagle that stirs up the nest and carries its young on its wings. It pictures the same tender care as Hosea 11:3 and 4, and shows that the image of a loving parent was part of Israel's earliest songs.

Admah and Zeboiim are named with Sodom and Gomorrah as examples of total overthrow in the LORD's fierce anger. Hosea 11:8 uses them to ask whether Israel should suffer the same fate, and it is the same verb that appears when God's heart is overturned.

Ephraim confesses that he was like an untrained calf, and the LORD answers that he is a precious son and a delightful child, and that His heart yearns for him. It is the nearest parallel to Hosea 11:8, and it shows that the same compassion was spoken by two prophets in two generations.

In all their distress He too was afflicted, and in His love and compassion He redeemed them and carried them. The verse describes the LORD sharing the suffering of His people in the exodus, which fits the way Hosea shows God as wounded by Israel's departure.

In the parable of the returning son, the father sees him while he is still far off, is filled with compassion, runs, embraces and kisses him. The story is Hosea 11 in narrative form, with the father who cannot give up his son and welcomes him home before he can speak.

God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. Hosea asks how God can give up Ephraim, and Paul shows that He gave up His own Son rather than abandon His people. It is the New Testament answer to the question of verse 8.

Those led by the Spirit are sons of God and receive the Spirit of sonship by whom we cry Abba Father. The child who ran away in Hosea becomes, in Christ, the child who is welcomed and can address God without fear.

Ephraim is a silly dove, calling out to Egypt and turning to Assyria. Hosea 11:11 takes up the same bird, the dove from Assyria, but now it comes home trembling to the LORD. The image of the wandering bird in chapter 7 is reversed in the promise of chapter 11.

study.oneStory:
The poem sits at the point where the Bible's story of sonship meets the Bible's story of sin. Adam is called the son of God in Luke's genealogy, and he was put out of the garden. Israel was called the LORD's firstborn son and was carried to the edge of the land and finally out of it again. Humanity's history is a chain of sons who run away, and Hosea 11 asks whether the Father will finally let them go. The answer, spoken here with great force, is no.

The chapter also looks back to the heart of the exodus. The rescue of Israel was an act of fatherly love before it was an act of power, and the later history of idolatry was a response to that love. Hosea recasts the whole story from Egypt to the exile as a family drama. What the law spoke of as covenant, Hosea speaks of as childhood, and the framing makes the final line of the story more than a legal settlement.

The chapter points forward to the great turn. The question of verse 8 cannot be left hanging, because to spare the guilty seems to deny justice and to punish them seems to deny love. The story's answer is that the Son takes the place of the sons. He passes through Egypt, takes up Israel's calling, is given up, and in His death the Father's justice and the Father's mercy meet. Paul calls this the demonstration of God's righteousness, Romans 3:25 and 26, and John calls it the reason for the gift of the Son, John 3:16.

The promised homecoming of verses 10 and 11 is also taken up and widened. The scattered children of God, John 11:52, come from every nation to the one who calls them, and the church inherits the language of sonship, Galatians 4:4 to 7. The new creation is the place where the Father dwells with His children, and the voice says that He will be their God and they will be His children, Revelation 21:7. The child once taught to walk is finally brought home, and the love that began the story is the love that ends it.

quiz.q: How does God remember His relationship with Israel in verses 1 to 4?

options.text: As a father who loved a child, called him out of Egypt, taught him to walk, and bent down to feed him.
options.note: Verses 1 to 4 use tender fatherly images of raising a child.

options.text: As a distant ruler with no affection for Israel.
options.note: The whole point is God's deep fatherly love, not distance.

options.text: As an employer paying wages for work done.
options.note: The relationship is family love, not a transaction.

options.text: As a stranger who barely knew them.
options.note: God knew and nurtured Israel from infancy.

quiz.q: What happens in God's heart in verse 8?

options.text: His compassion is stirred and His heart recoils, so He will not carry out the full fury of His wrath.
options.note: Verse 8 reveals compassion overriding deserved judgment.

options.text: He grows even more determined to destroy them utterly.
options.note: The opposite; His compassion holds back the full fury.

options.text: He becomes indifferent to Israel's fate.
options.note: He is anything but indifferent; His heart is deeply moved.

options.text: He decides sin does not matter.
options.note: Sin still matters; mercy triumphs without denying justice.

quiz.q: Why does God give for His mercy in verse 9?

options.text: Because He is God and not man, the Holy One among them.
options.note: Verse 9 grounds His constant mercy in His being God, not fickle man.

options.text: Because Israel had finally earned it.
options.note: The mercy flows from God's character, not Israel's merit.

options.text: Because the sin was not really serious.
options.note: The sin was grave; the mercy is greater and rooted in God.

options.text: Because He had forgotten their idolatry.
options.note: He remembers it fully, yet chooses compassion.

quiz.q: How is verse 1 fulfilled in the New Testament?

options.text: Matthew 2:15 applies out of Egypt I called My son to Jesus, the true and faithful Son.
options.note: Christ recapitulates and redeems Israel's story as God's Son.

options.text: It is never referred to in the New Testament.
options.note: Matthew explicitly cites it as fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: It refers only to a future political nation.
options.note: The New Testament applies it to Christ Himself.

options.text: It predicts a return of Israel to literal slavery.
options.note: It is fulfilled in Christ called out of Egypt, not renewed slavery.

quiz.q: How does God's refusal to give His people up point to the cross?

options.text: At the cross God satisfies His justice in His Son, so He can righteously refuse to give His people up.
options.note: Wrath is borne by Christ so mercy can triumph, Romans 3:25 to 26.

options.text: It shows God simply ignores justice when He feels like it.
options.note: God does not ignore justice; He satisfies it in Christ.

options.text: It means no one ever faces judgment.
options.note: Judgment is real; Christ bears it for His people.

options.text: It has no connection to the cross.
options.note: The cross is where wrath and mercy meet, resolving verse 8.

questions: God remembers teaching Israel to walk and stooping to feed him. How does picturing God's fatherly tenderness toward you change the way you relate to Him?
Israel kept running from the God who loved them. Where do you find yourself drifting from God even as He keeps calling you?
God's compassion recoiled at giving His people up. When have you most needed to hear that God will not let you go?
God's mercy is trustworthy because He is God and not man. How does the constancy of God's love steady you when your own love for Him wavers?
The wrath God held back was ultimately borne by Christ. How does the cross deepen your understanding of the words, How can I give you up?

translationNotes.note: Out of Egypt I called My son is cited in Matthew 2:15 as fulfilled in Christ, the true Son of God.
The BSB follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew reads the more they called them, the more they went from them, but the sense of persistent turning away is the same.
I will not come in wrath may also be rendered I will not come against their cities.
